earlier_scan.source_named: Israel, Motchakon. 1979. A grammar of the Kuvi language: with texts and vocabulary. Trivandrum: Dravidian Linguistics Assoc. (444pp, not online). Schulze 1911 grammar READ on archive.org: no stress/accent statement found in it

sources.citation: Reddy, Joy. 1979. Kuvi Grammar. (CIIL Grammar Series.) Mysore: Central Institute of Indian Languages. xii+145 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Ch. 1 Phonology (pp. 8-48: inventory, contrasts, allophones, length, nasalization, gemination, clusters) names only length and nasalization as 'co-occurring features'; the word 'stress' does not occur anywhere in the book (scanned verified against page scan).

sources.citation: Schulze, F. V. P. 1911. A grammar of the Kuvi language, with copious examples. Madras: Graves, Cookson & Co.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Nothing. Ch. II 'Alphabet' gives letter values and remarks on 'abrupt' (glottalized) pronunciation of verb roots; no accent/stress statement (confirms earlier scan).

sources.citation: Reddy, B. Ramakrishna, Susheela P. Upadhyaya & Joy Reddy. 1974. Kuvi Phonetic Reader. (CIIL Phonetic Reader Series 11.) Mysore: CIIL. xi+77 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Describes segments, length ('Length occurs with all vowels'), nasalization, juncture-conditioned allophones and an Oriya-based orthography; no stress/accent statement.

sources.citation: Anand, R. Selvin. 2002. Kuvi. In B. P. Mahapatra et al. (eds.), Linguistic Survey of India, Special Studies: Orissa, 553-574. Kolkata: Language Division, Office of the Registrar General.
sources.note: Silent on stress: 'Kuvi language has 27 segmental phonemes (5 vowels and 22 consonants) and 2 supra-segmental phonemes.. Two suprasegmental features, namely, length and nasalisation are found to occur in this [language]'. Data from Laxmipur (northern/Rayagada dialect).

sources.citation: Rajendran, S. & S. Boopathy. 2002. Khond/Kondh. In Linguistic Survey of India, Special Studies: Orissa, 476-496. Kolkata: Language Division.
sources.note: Nothing on stress (inventory, allophones, distribution, clusters only). Census 'Khond/Kondh' covers Kui-Kuvi speech generally.

sources.citation: Behera, Laxmidhar & Jagannath Dash. 2026. 'Kui' and 'Kuvi' Kondhs of Odisha: a comparative study of their language and culture. IOSR Journal of Humanities and Social Science 31(5) ser. 4: 13-22. doi:10.9790/0837-3105041322
sources.note: 'Stress in Kuvi is generally non-phonemic, and intonation patterns are used primarily for pragmatic and discourse-level functions.' Anthropological overview without data or page-cited sources; bibliography contains a fabricated reference (Anderson & Harrison 2008 'South Munda Languages: Kui and Kuvi'), so not usable as a description of record. No placement statement anyway.

sources.note: Fullest modern grammar of Kuvi; Google Books snippets prove it speaks of 'a stressed syllable' and 'syllables carrying phonetic stress', so it almost certainly states where (phonetic, non-phonemic) stress falls. HathiTrust has it digitized search-only (Record 000122266, uva.x002705745); Harvard Widener PL4706.I87x 1979 eligible for a library scan.

sources.note: Snippet: 'KUI [dialects.. Kui, Konda-Kui, Manda-Kui, Kui-Kuvi]. Madhya Pradesh (India). • Primary stress falls on the initial syllable.' This is the KUI entry (kuii1252), which merely lists 'Kui-Kuvi' among alternate/dialect names; there is no separate Kuvi entry. StressTyp2 SQL dump held by the project has only an ISO row for kxv, no Kuvi record; WALS (held by the project) has no stress features coded for Kuvi.
